pos: v. (to make firm, to settle, to confirm; rendering Hebrew qum and kun, Greek histemi and sterizo)
etymology: From the Latin stabilio, to make stable, from sto, to stand, through Old French establir. The KJV also uses the older form stablish. Hebrew qum is to raise up and cause to stand; kun, to set firm.
biblical_def: To establish is to make a thing stand, and in Scripture the subject of the verb is almost always God. He establishes covenants: “And I, behold, I establish my covenant with you, and with your seed after you” (Genesis 9:9) — the pronoun is doubled for emphasis, and Noah is not asked to agree to terms. The covenant stands because God stands behind it, which is what distinguishes a biblical covenant from a contract between equals. Man's part is to ask for the establishing rather than to supply it: “establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it” (Psalm 90:17) — the request repeated in the same breath, by a man who has just spent a psalm on how briefly hands work at all. Proverbs gives the ordinary mechanism: “Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established” (Proverbs 16:3), where the committing is ours and the establishing is his, and the thing steadied is not the circumstances but the mind. And Paul uses the word at the hinge of his argument on justification: “Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law” (Romans 3:31). Justification by faith alone does not abolish the law; it is the only doctrine that ever honoured it, since in the cross the law's full penalty was paid rather than waived.
webster_summary: To make firm; to cause to stand. God establishes his covenant unilaterally, Moses asks him to establish the work of our hands, and Paul says justification by faith establishes the law rather than voiding it.
webster_full: ESTABLISH, v.t. [Fr. establir; L. stabilio, from sto, to stand.] To set and fix firmly or unalterably; to settle permanently.
2. To found permanently; to erect and fix or settle; as, to establish a colony or an empire.
3. To enact or decree by authority and for permanence; to ordain; to appoint; as, to establish laws.
4. To confirm; to fix or settle in opinion; as, to establish a man in the truth.
5. To make good; to prove and cause to be accepted as true; as, to establish a fact or a doctrine.
corruption_summary: Justification by faith is charged with making the law void — the antinomian error Paul answers with an emphatic God forbid — while men attempt to establish by effort what only God can settle.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 3:31 answers a charge as old as the gospel: that a righteousness reckoned by faith apart from works of law leaves the law with no standing. Paul's reply is that the opposite is true. The law is established at Calvary precisely because it was not relaxed there — God did not lower the requirement, he satisfied it, so that he might be just and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus. Antinomianism, which treats grace as release from obligation, and legalism, which treats obedience as the ground of acceptance, both fail to see what the cross did to the law. The believer is not under the law as a covenant of works and remains under it as a rule of life, which is the ordinary Reformed distinction and the answer to both errors.

The principle to recover is the direction of the establishing. Psalm 90 is a psalm about brevity — we spend our years as a tale that is told, our days are threescore years and ten — and its last request is that God would make the work of such short-lived hands stand. Moses does not ask for longer life or larger work; he asks that what is done should last, and he asks twice. Every believer who has watched good work undone knows the prayer. Nothing a man builds outlives him unless God establishes it, and the request is one God delights to grant.
roots_summary: Hebrew qum is to arise, to cause to stand, used of establishing a covenant; kun is to be firm or fixed. Greek histemi is to make stand; sterizo, to prop or strengthen.
roots_lines: Hebrew qum (H6965) — to rise, to raise up, to establish; the verb of establishing a covenant.
Hebrew kun (H3559) — to be firm, set upright, prepared; established thoughts and an established throne.
Greek histemi (G2476) — to make to stand; we establish the law, Romans 3:31.
Greek sterizo (G4741) — to set fast, to strengthen, to stablish; the Lord shall stablish you.
Greek bebaioo (G950) — to confirm, make sure; God stablisheth us with you in Christ.
usage: Of a covenant God establishes alone: I establish my covenant with you (Genesis 9:9).
Of the prayer for lasting work: establish thou the work of our hands upon us (Psalm 90:17).
Of faith upholding the law: yea, we establish the law (Romans 3:31).
scriptures: Genesis 9:9
And I, behold, I establish my covenant with you, and with your seed after you;
Psalm 90:17
And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
Deuteronomy 8:18
But thou shalt remember the LORD thy God: for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth, that he may establish his covenant which he sware unto thy fathers, as it is this day.
Proverbs 16:3
Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established.

pos: v. (to carry through to completion; to fulfil what was promised or vowed; rendering Hebrew asah and qum, Greek epiteleo and poieo)
etymology: From Old French parfournir, to complete or furnish through, from par (thoroughly) and fournir, to furnish. The buried sense is not display but completion — to perform a thing is to carry it all the way out.
biblical_def: To perform in Scripture is to bring a word to its accomplishment, and the doctrine turns on who is doing it. Of God it is stated as a settled character: he is watching over his own speech, “for I will hasten my word to perform it” (Jeremiah 1:12) — spoken to a young prophet who had just objected that he was a child, and given in the form of a pun on the almond tree, the watching-tree that wakes first in the year. Abraham's faith is defined by the same verb: he was “fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform” (Romans 4:21). Faith, in Paul's definition, is confidence in a promiser's competence, not optimism about outcomes. The best-known instance is Paul's confidence for a church: “he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6) — the beginning and the completing are both God's, which is the doctrine of perseverance stated as a pastoral certainty. Of man the verb appears as vow-keeping, and it costs: “I have sworn, and I will perform it, that I will keep thy righteous judgments” (Psalm 119:106). To swear is easy and to perform is the whole of the matter, which is why Ecclesiastes warns that it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay.
webster_summary: To carry through to completion. God hastens his word to perform it and completes the work he began; faith is being persuaded he is able to perform; and a man's vow is nothing until performed.
webster_full: PERFORM, v.t. [L. per and formo, or Fr. parfournir, to complete.] To do; to execute; to accomplish; to carry through to the end.
2. To execute; to discharge; as, to perform a duty or a promise.
3. To fulfil; as, to perform a covenant or a vow.
4. PERFORM, v.i. To do; to act a part; as, the actor performed well.
5. PERFORMANCE, n. Execution or completion of any thing; a deed or action done.
corruption_summary: Philippians 1:6 is applied as a general reassurance about a man's plans, when it is a promise about God's work of salvation — and vows are made lightly because performing them is no longer thought to matter.
corruption_paragraphs: Philippians 1:6 is one of the most misapplied verses in common use, pressed into service to assure people that whatever project or ambition God has supposedly begun in them will succeed. Paul is speaking of a good work in a specific sense: the salvation of the Philippians, begun when the gospel came to them by a riverside and a jailer's house, and completed at the day of Jesus Christ. That is why the verse is a comfort. It rests the believer's perseverance on God's completion rather than on his own consistency, and it is the ordinary Reformed doctrine that those whom God effectually calls he also keeps. Applied to careers and plans it becomes a promise God never made and experience will break.

The principle to recover is the seriousness of performing what is vowed. Psalm 119:106 is a man binding himself with an oath to keep God's judgments, and Scripture treats such words as debts. When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools (Ecclesiastes 5:4). Membership promises, marriage vows, and ordination pledges are made in an age that has largely stopped believing words create obligations, and the wreckage is visible. The remedy is not fewer vows but performed ones, and the model is God himself, who watches over his word to do it.
roots_summary: Hebrew asah is to do or make; qum, to raise up, is used of performing a word or oath. Greek epiteleo is to complete; poieo, to do.
roots_lines: Hebrew asah (H6213) — to do, make, accomplish; the common verb of performing a thing.
Hebrew qum (H6965) — to raise up, to make good; used of performing an oath or word.
Hebrew shaqad (H8245) — to watch, to hasten; the pun on the almond tree in Jeremiah 1:11-12.
Greek epiteleo (G2005) — to complete, to finish; will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.
Greek poieo (G4160) — to do, to make; the general verb of doing what was said.
usage: Of God watching over his own word: I will hasten my word to perform it (Jeremiah 1:12).
Of faith defined: what he had promised, he was able also to perform (Romans 4:21).
Of a vow made and to be kept: I have sworn, and I will perform it (Psalm 119:106).
scriptures: Jeremiah 1:12
Then said the LORD unto me, Thou hast well seen: for I will hasten my word to perform it.
Romans 4:21
And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform.
Philippians 1:6
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:
Psalm 119:106
I have sworn, and I will perform it, that I will keep thy righteous judgments.

pos: v. (to withhold a deserved stroke; to refrain from destroying; rendering Hebrew chamal and chus, Greek pheidomai)
etymology: From the Saxon sparian, to spare or save. Hebrew chamal means to pity or spare; chus, to have compassion, literally to let the eye flow. To spare in Hebrew is an act of the eye before it is an act of the hand.
biblical_def: To spare is to withhold a stroke that was deserved or intended, and Scripture's use of the word reaches its centre in one verse: “He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). The whole argument for Christian assurance is compressed into an inference from the greater to the lesser. God did not spare where sparing would have cost him most; therefore no lesser gift will be withheld. The Greek echoes Genesis 22, where Abraham is told thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son — and the difference is that at the last moment a ram was provided for Isaac, and for Christ there was no substitute, because he was the substitute. God is also said to spare, and the image is domestic: “I will spare them, as a man spareth his own son that serveth him” (Malachi 3:17), spoken of those who feared the LORD and spake often one to another. Jonah ends on a question about sparing a pagan city of six score thousand who could not discern their right hand from their left (Jonah 4:11). And Proverbs applies the word to a father's rod: “He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes” (Proverbs 13:24) — sparing is not always kindness.
webster_summary: To withhold a deserved stroke. God spared not his own Son, and every lesser gift follows from it; he spares his people as a father his son; and Proverbs warns that a spared rod is not love.
webster_full: SPARE, v.t. [Sax. sparian.] To use frugally; not to be profuse; to use with moderation.
2. To save or withhold from any particular use or occupation; as, to spare time from business.
3. To omit; to forbear; as, to spare a rebuke.
4. To use tenderly; to treat with pity and forbearance; to forbear to afflict, punish or destroy.
5. To part with without inconvenience; as, he can spare a shilling.
corruption_summary: Sparing is treated as the whole of love, so that discipline of children and church alike is thought unkind — and God's not sparing his own Son is softened into a tragedy rather than a purpose.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 13:24 states an unfashionable principle in the plainest terms: withholding correction is hatred, and correcting early is love. Scripture's doctrine of discipline is not harshness — fathers are expressly commanded not to provoke their children to wrath, and correction is betimes, that is, early and proportionate, not violent or late. But the modern assumption that any correction wounds a child inverts the verse and produces exactly the child the proverb warns of. The same instinct empties church discipline, which Scripture commands for the good of the offender, and turns pastoral care into unconditional affirmation. Hebrews 12 makes the argument decisive: the Lord chastens whom he loves, and a son not chastened is not a son. The other softening runs the other way. Romans 8:32 is sometimes preached as though the cross were something that happened to God rather than something he purposed, but the verb is active: he… delivered him up. The Father gave, the Son gave himself, and the atonement was not an accident of history but a definite and effectual purpose to save a definite people.

The principle to recover is the argument in Romans 8:32, which is the strongest logic in the Bible for a doubting Christian. The reasoning is not that God is generally kind but that a specific and infinitely costly thing has already been done. If the Son was not spared, no argument remains for supposing that anything smaller will be denied to those for whom he was given. Assurance built here does not depend on a believer's feelings, and Paul goes on to say that nothing in the whole creation shall separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
roots_summary: Hebrew chamal is to spare or pity; chus, to have compassion, literally of the eye. Greek pheidomai is to spare or forbear, the verb of Romans 8:32.
roots_lines: Hebrew chamal (H2550) — to spare, to have compassion; used of Pharaoh's daughter and of God.
Hebrew chus (H2347) — to pity, to spare; literally to let the eye flow with compassion.
Greek pheidomai (G5339) — to spare, to refrain; he that spared not his own Son.
Greek paradidomi (G3860) — to deliver up, to hand over; the Father's act in Romans 8:32.
Hebrew chasak (H2820) — to withhold; thou hast not withheld thy son, Genesis 22:12.
usage: Of the Son not spared: he that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all (Romans 8:32).
Of God sparing his own: I will spare them, as a man spareth his own son that serveth him (Malachi 3:17).
Of a rod not to be spared: he that spareth his rod hateth his son (Proverbs 13:24).
scriptures: Romans 8:32
He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?
Malachi 3:17
And they shall be mine, saith the LORD of hosts, in that day when I make up my jewels; and I will spare them, as a man spareth his own son that serveth him.

Jonah 4:11
And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?

pos: v. (to come to with a purpose, in blessing or in judgment; rendering Hebrew paqad, Greek episkeptomai)
etymology: From the Latin visito, to go to see, from video, to see. Hebrew paqad is far stronger than the English social sense: it means to attend to, to muster, to reckon with — a visitation is an inspection with consequences.
biblical_def: To visit in Scripture is to come with a purpose and to act, and the same word covers mercy and judgment. In mercy: “the LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did unto Sarah as he had spoken” (Genesis 21:1) — the visitation is Isaac, and the verse repeats as he had said and as he had spoken because the point is a promise kept after twenty-five years and a laugh. Zacharias uses it of the incarnation: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people” (Luke 1:68) — God visiting in person, after four hundred silent years. In judgment the same verb: “I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me” (Exodus 20:5). The qualifier matters — of them that hate me — and the next verse promises mercy unto thousands of them that love him, so the ratio is not symmetrical. Then James turns the word toward the church's duty and makes it the test of religion: “Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (James 1:27). We are to visit as God visits — going to people, in their affliction, and doing something.
webster_summary: To come with purpose and act — in mercy or in judgment. The LORD visited Sarah, visited and redeemed his people in Christ, visits iniquity on those who hate him; and pure religion visits the fatherless and widows.
webster_full: VISIT, v.t. [L. visito, from video, to see.] To go or come to see; to attend; as, to visit a friend.
2. To go or come to see for inspection, examination, correction of abuses; as, to visit the churches.
3. To send good or evil to, as a punishment or blessing; to bless or afflict.
4. In Scripture, to send judgments; I will visit their transgression with the rod, Ps. 89.
5. Also, to come to in mercy; the Lord visited Sarah, Gen. 21.
corruption_summary: Exodus 20:5 is read as God punishing children for their parents' sins, ignoring the clause that limits it — while James 1:27 is quoted for social action detached from the second half of the same verse.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 20:5 is a favourite text of objectors and is regularly quoted without its qualifier. The visiting falls on them that hate me — that is, on children who continue in their fathers' hatred of God, not on innocents charged with ancestral guilt. Scripture states the individual principle elsewhere with no ambiguity: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father (Ezekiel 18:20). What the second commandment describes is the observable fact that sin runs in households, that idolatry is taught by example, and that a generation may inherit its parents' hatred along with their furniture. And the promise attached is far larger than the threat: mercy unto thousands of them that love God and keep his commandments. James 1:27 has the opposite problem. It is enlisted for programmes of social concern with its second clause quietly dropped, though the verse defines pure religion as both visiting the afflicted and keeping oneself unspotted from the world. A church that does one and abandons the other has not obeyed half the verse; it has failed the definition.

The principle to recover is that God's visiting is the model for ours. He does not send word to Sarah; he visits her. He does not merely pity his people; he visits and redeems them in the flesh. James therefore uses the same verb for orphans and widows, and the choice is deliberate. Visiting in the biblical sense is bodily presence with intent to act — going to where the affliction is, at cost, and doing something about it. It cannot be done at a distance and it cannot be delegated to an institution without ceasing to be what the word means.
roots_summary: Hebrew paqad is to attend to, muster, appoint, or reckon with — hence to visit in blessing or judgment. Greek episkeptomai is to look upon, to care for; the root of episkopos, overseer.
roots_lines: Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, muster, attend to, punish; the great verb of divine visitation.
Hebrew pequddah (H6486) — visitation, oversight, reckoning; the day of visitation.
Greek episkeptomai (G1980) — to look upon, visit, care for; James 1:27 and Matthew 25:36.
Greek episkope (G1984) — visitation, oversight; the time of thy visitation, Luke 19:44.
Greek episkopos (G1985) — an overseer, bishop; one whose office is to visit and inspect.
usage: Of a promise kept: the LORD visited Sarah as he had said (Genesis 21:1).
Of the incarnation: he hath visited and redeemed his people (Luke 1:68).
Of the test of pure religion: to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction (James 1:27).

Exodus 20:5

Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;
Luke 7:16
And there came a fear on all: and they glorified God, saying, That a great prophet is risen up among us; and, That God hath visited his people.

pos: v. (to succeed, to be carried forward favourably; rendering Hebrew tsalach, Greek euodoo)
etymology: From the Latin prospero, from pro spere, according to hope. Greek euodoo is literally to have a good journey, from eu and hodos, a way — to prosper is to have one's road go well.
biblical_def: To prosper in Scripture is to be carried forward by God, and the Bible is careful about where it locates prospering. Of Joseph in slavery: “his master saw that the LORD was with him, and that the LORD made all that he did to prosper in his hand” (Genesis 39:3) — the man is a purchased slave in a foreign house, and the word is used of him without irony. Prospering is not the absence of hardship but the presence of God in it. Proverbs states the moral condition negatively: “He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Proverbs 28:13) — concealment blocks it, and the way out is confession joined to forsaking. John's greeting sets the measure: “Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth” (3 John 2) — the soul's prosperity is the yardstick, and a man whose outward life exceeded it would be in danger rather than in blessing. The word's greatest use is in the suffering-servant chapter: after the LORD has bruised him and made his soul an offering for sin, “the pleasure of the LORD shall prosper in his hand” (Isaiah 53:10). The crucifixion is the place where the word prosper is used of God's purposes reaching their end.
webster_summary: To be carried forward favourably. Joseph prospers as a slave, hidden sin blocks prospering, John measures outward prosperity by the soul's — and Isaiah says God's pleasure prospered in the hand of a bruised servant.
webster_full: PROSPER, v.t. [L. prospero, from prosperus, from pro and spero, to hope.] To favor; to render successful.
2. PROSPER, v.i. To be successful; to succeed; as, the works of the diligent prosper.
3. To grow or increase; to thrive; to make gain; as, to prosper in business.
4. PROSPERITY, n. Advance or gain in any thing good or desirable; successful progress in any business or enterprise.
5. In Scripture, whatsoever he doeth shall prosper, Ps. 1; he that covereth his sins shall not prosper, Prov. 28.
corruption_summary: Prosperity teaching makes health and wealth the guaranteed portion of faith, and 3 John 2 is its favourite proof-text — though the verse makes the soul the measure and Isaiah 53 makes a bruised servant the pattern.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity gospel takes 3 John 2 as a promise of material increase, which requires ignoring both the form and the content of the sentence. It is a greeting, of the ordinary kind found at the head of ancient letters, and its wish is bounded by a comparison: even as thy soul prospereth. John is praying that Gaius's outward circumstances would match his inward state, which is a compliment to Gaius and a terrifying prayer to pray over most people. The wider teaching fails on Scripture's own examples. Joseph prospered in a prison. Paul, who had learned to be full and to be hungry, wrote from chains. And the servant of Isaiah 53, in whose hand God's pleasure prospers, is despised, rejected, wounded, and cut off out of the land of the living.

The principle to recover is Proverbs 28:13, which is the plainest verse in the Bible on what actually obstructs a life. It is not lack of opportunity or of faith but concealment. Covering sin does not remove it; it only prevents mercy, because mercy is promised to the man who does two things — confesses and forsakes. David describes the covering years in Psalm 32: his bones waxed old, God's hand was heavy upon him, and his moisture was turned into the drought of summer, until he acknowledged his sin and the guilt was forgiven. Prospering, in Scripture, usually begins with an honest sentence.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsalach is to rush forward, to advance, to succeed — the Spirit of the LORD is said to come mightily upon a man with the same verb. Greek euodoo is to have a good journey.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsalach (H6743) — to advance, push forward, prosper; used of Joseph and of the servant's work.
Hebrew shalah (H7951) — to be at ease, prosperous; the prosperity of the wicked in the Psalms.
Hebrew shalom (H7965) — peace, wholeness, welfare; the broader word for a life going well.
Greek euodoo (G2137) — to have a good journey, to prosper; the verb of 3 John 2.
Greek eudokia (G2107) — good pleasure; akin to the pleasure of the LORD of Isaiah 53:10.
usage: Of a slave prospering: the LORD made all that he did to prosper in his hand (Genesis 39:3).
Of concealment blocking mercy: he that covereth his sins shall not prosper (Proverbs 28:13).
Of God's purpose in a bruised servant: the pleasure of the LORD shall prosper in his hand (Isaiah 53:10).

pos: v. and n. (to get free of a danger; a way out; rendering Hebrew malat and palat, Greek ekpheugo and ekbasis)
etymology: From Old French eschaper, from a late Latin excappare, to slip out of one's cape — to leave the cloak in the pursuer's hand and get away. The image of a garment abandoned to escape is exactly Joseph's in Genesis 39.
biblical_def: Escape in Scripture is urgent, provided, and in one case impossible. It is urgent at Sodom, where the angels give Lot a command with no room in it: “Escape for thy life; look not behind thee, neither stay thou in all the plain; escape to the mountain, lest thou be consumed” (Genesis 19:17). Four imperatives, and one of them was disobeyed by his wife. It is provided in temptation: “God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it” (1 Corinthians 10:13) — and the promise is precise. The way out is made with the temptation, so it exists at the time it is needed, and its purpose is stated as endurance rather than avoidance. The Psalter sings of escape already granted: “Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped” (Psalm 124:7) — and the deliverance is credited to the snare being broken, not to the bird's strength. Against all of these Hebrews sets the one danger with no exit: “How shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation” (Hebrews 2:3). The verse is a question because there is no answer to it. Neglect is enough; no active rejection is required.
webster_summary: To get free of danger. Lot is commanded to escape with four imperatives; God makes a way to escape with every temptation; the soul escapes as a bird when the snare is broken — and Hebrews asks how we shall escape if we neglect so great salvation.
webster_full: ESCAPE, v.t. [Fr. echapper; It. scappare.] To flee from and avoid; to get out of the way; to shun.
2. To pass without harm; as, the ship escaped the storm.
3. ESCAPE, v.i. To flee, shun and be secure from danger; to avoid an evil.
4. ESCAPE, n. Flight to shun danger or injury; the act of fleeing from danger.
5. Excuse; subterfuge; evasion. In Scripture, a way to escape, 1 Cor. 10.
corruption_summary: 1 Corinthians 10:13 is quoted as a promise that God will not give more than a man can handle — a saying about circumstances the verse never makes, since it speaks of temptation and promises endurance rather than relief.
corruption_paragraphs: The popular version of this verse — God will not give you more than you can handle — is not what Paul wrote and does not survive contact with 2 Corinthians 1:8, where the same apostle says he was pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that he despaired even of life. The promise of 1 Corinthians 10:13 is about temptation, that is, solicitation to sin, and it makes three specific claims: the temptation is common to man, God limits it, and he supplies a way of escape. It does not promise that afflictions will stay within a believer's capacity. In fact Paul says the crushing weight he bore was given that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead. Comfort misquoted collapses at the moment it is most needed.

The principle to recover is the weight of Hebrews 2:3. The word is neglect, and it names the way most people are lost — not by argument or defiance but by never getting round to it. The letter is written to people who had heard, who had been confirmed in it by eyewitnesses, and who were drifting; the previous verse spoke of letting things slip. There is no answer to the question how shall we escape, because the salvation neglected is the only escape there is. A man who declines a lifeboat has not thereby found a better one.
roots_summary: Hebrew malat is to slip away, to be delivered; palat, to bring to safety. Greek ekpheugo is to flee out of; ekbasis, a way out, the word in 1 Corinthians 10:13.

pos: v. (to argue a cause at law; to contend on behalf of or against; rendering Hebrew rib, Greek krino in the forensic sense)
etymology: From Old French plaidier, to go to law, from late Latin placitum, a decree or plea. Hebrew rib is a lawsuit or controversy — the prophets' standard form is the covenant lawsuit, in which God pleads against his people.
biblical_def: To plead in Scripture is a courtroom word, and God is the most frequent litigant. He pleads against his own people: “Wherefore I will yet plead with you, saith the LORD, and with your children's children will I plead” (Jeremiah 2:9) — the sentence is a summons, and the whole chapter is a covenant lawsuit charging Israel with exchanging a fountain of living waters for broken cisterns. Isaiah sets the scene formally: “The LORD standeth up to plead, and standeth to judge the people” (Isaiah 3:13) — and it is worth noting that God is described as standing, which in a courtroom is the posture of the advocate. He also commands the pleading of others' causes as a matter of religion: “Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow” (Isaiah 1:17). The widow's difficulty in an ancient court was that she had no man to speak for her, and God requires his people to be that man. The Psalter asks God to take the same office for the believer: “Judge me, O God, and plead my cause against an ungodly nation” (Psalm 43:1) — a request that only makes sense because the Judge is also willing to be the Advocate, which is precisely what the New Testament says he is.
webster_summary: To argue a cause at law. God pleads against his people in covenant lawsuit, commands his people to plead for the widow, and is asked to plead the believer's cause — being at once the Judge and the Advocate.
webster_full: PLEAD, v.i. [Fr. plaider.] In a general sense, to argue in support of a claim, or in defense against the claim of another.
2. In law, to present an answer to the declaration of a plaintiff; to deny the plaintiff's declaration.
3. To urge reasons for or against; to attempt to persuade by argument or supplication.
4. PLEAD, v.t. To discuss and defend; as, to plead a cause.
5. To allege or adduce in proof, support or vindication; as, to plead one's cause; to plead the merits of Christ.
corruption_summary: Advocacy for the defenceless is either abandoned to the state, or redefined by frameworks that assign standing by group rather than by the biblical categories of the widow, the fatherless, and the stranger.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 1:17 names four duties and they are specific: seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow. These are not abstractions but courtroom acts, and the persons named share one feature — they have no advocate. Two failures follow the loss of this. The first hands the whole matter to institutions, so that individual Christians no longer know a widow well enough to plead for anyone. The second replaces Scripture's categories with the oppressor-oppressed binary of critical race theory and related frameworks, in which standing is assigned by group identity rather than by actual defencelessness. Biblical anthropology has no room for that: all are one in Adam and, in Christ, one body, and Leviticus forbids partiality toward the poor as firmly as toward the mighty.

The principle to recover is that the Judge is the Advocate. Psalm 43:1 asks God both to judge and to plead, which would be a scandal in any human court and is the glory of the gospel. John states it plainly: if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1) — the word is parakletos, one called alongside to plead a cause. The believer stands before a bench where the one who will pass sentence has already argued his case and paid his fine, and this is why the Christian may ask to be judged rather than dreading it.
roots_summary: Hebrew rib is to contend, to conduct a lawsuit; the noun is a controversy or covenant lawsuit. Greek parakletos is one called alongside to plead, the Advocate.
roots_lines: Hebrew rib (H7378) — to strive, contend, plead a case; the verb of the prophetic covenant lawsuit.
Hebrew rib (H7379) — the noun: a controversy, a suit at law; the LORD hath a controversy with his people.
Hebrew shaphat (H8199) — to judge, to pronounce sentence; paired with pleading in Isaiah 3:13.
Greek parakletos (G3875) — one called alongside; an advocate; of Christ and of the Holy Ghost.
Greek entugchano (G1793) — to intercede, to plead with; he ever liveth to make intercession.
usage: Of God's lawsuit with his people: I will yet plead with you, saith the LORD (Jeremiah 2:9).
Of the duty to the defenceless: judge the fatherless, plead for the widow (Isaiah 1:17).
Of the believer's request: judge me, O God, and plead my cause (Psalm 43:1).

pos: v. (to rouse from sleep or from death; to become alert; rendering Hebrew quts and ur, Greek egeiro and eknepho)
etymology: From the Saxon awacian, to wake up. Hebrew quts is to awake from sleep, and is the ordinary word used for the resurrection in Daniel 12; ur is to rouse or stir up, used of rousing oneself and of God rousing his arm.
biblical_def: Awake in Scripture runs from ordinary morning to the resurrection of the dead. Daniel gives the plainest Old Testament statement of a general resurrection: “many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2). Two destinations, both everlasting, both entered by awaking — a verse that annihilationism and universalism must each explain away. The Psalter makes the same waking a satisfaction: “As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness” (Psalm 17:15) — the only satisfaction Scripture promises without qualification, and it is on the far side of sleep. Paul uses the imperative twice for the spiritually dull. To the Corinthians, arguing about the resurrection while keeping bad company: “Awake to righteousness, and sin not; for some have not the knowledge of God: I speak this to your shame” (1 Corinthians 15:34) — the verb is properly to sober up. And to the Ephesians he quotes what appears to be an early Christian hymn: “Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light” (Ephesians 5:14). The command is addressed to the dead, which is the standing puzzle of gospel preaching and its standing answer: the command is issued, and Christ supplies what the command requires.
webster_summary: To rouse from sleep or death. Daniel makes awaking the resurrection to two everlasting destinations; the Psalter finds satisfaction only after it; Paul commands the dead to awake, and says Christ shall give the light.
webster_full: AWAKE, v.t. [Sax. awacian.] To rouse from sleep.
2. To excite from a state resembling sleep, as from death, stupidity or inaction; to put into action, or new life.
3. AWAKE, v.i. To cease to sleep; to come from a state of natural sleep.
4. To rouse from a state of inaction; to be invigorated with new life; as, the mind awakes from its stupidity.
5. AWAKE, a. Not sleeping; in a state of vigilance or action.
corruption_summary: The command to the spiritually dead is treated as proof that they have the power to obey it — and Daniel's two everlasting destinations are softened by annihilationism and universalism alike.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 5:14 is often used to argue that since God commands sinners to awake, they must be able to. The inference does not hold, and Scripture supplies the counter-examples itself: Christ commanded a man with a withered hand to stretch it forth, and a four-days-dead man to come forth, and in both cases the power came with the command. This is the Reformed doctrine of effectual calling. God's commands reveal our duty, not our ability; the fall left man's whole nature — mind and will together — unable to come, and the gospel call is accompanied in the elect by a power that raises. The last clause of the verse is the key: and Christ shall give thee light. The sleeper does not manufacture the dawn. Daniel 12:2 is meanwhile pressed from two sides. Annihilationism must make everlasting contempt a completed extinction, and universalism must make it temporary; but the verse sets the two destinies in exact parallel, and the same word governs both. Whatever weight everlasting carries for the life it carries for the contempt.

The principle to recover is Psalm 17:15, which is one of the most quietly devastating verses in the Psalter. David has just described men of the world which have their portion in this life, whose bellies God fills and who leave their substance to their babes — a fair description of a comfortable life. Against it he sets a single line: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness. Not before. The believer's satisfaction is deferred by design, and the deferral is not a defect in the Christian life but its shape.
roots_summary: Hebrew quts is to awake from sleep, used of the resurrection in Daniel 12:2; ur is to rouse or stir up. Greek egeiro is to raise; eknepho, to sober up out of a stupor.
roots_lines: Hebrew quts (H6974) — to awake, to be roused; the resurrection verb of Daniel 12:2.
Hebrew ur (H5782) — to rouse, to stir up; awake, O sword, and awake, awake, put on strength.
Greek egeiro (G1453) — to raise, to awaken; used of waking from sleep and of resurrection.
Greek eknepho (G1594) — to become sober, to wake out of a stupor; 1 Corinthians 15:34.
Greek anistemi (G450) — to stand up, to arise; arise from the dead, Ephesians 5:14.
usage: Of the general resurrection: many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake (Daniel 12:2).

pos: v. (to eat up greedily; to consume or destroy; rendering Hebrew akal, Greek katapino and katesthio)
etymology: From the Latin devoro, to swallow down, from de and voro, to eat greedily. The Greek katapino is literally to drink down — the picture is of swallowing whole rather than of eating in the ordinary way.
biblical_def: To devour is to consume utterly, and Scripture applies it to three devourers. First, the adversary: “Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5:8). Four things in that verse are worth holding together — sobriety and vigilance are commanded, the enemy is real, he is as a roaring lion rather than one, and he is seeking, which means he has to look. He is not omniscient and he is not omnipresent, and the next verse says he is to be resisted stedfast in the faith. Second, the oppressor: Proverbs describes “a generation, whose teeth are as swords, and their jaw teeth as knives, to devour the poor from off the earth, and the needy from among men” (Proverbs 30:14). The metaphor is deliberate; economic predation is described in the vocabulary of a beast. Third, and most soberly, God: Hebrews warns of “a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries” (Hebrews 10:27). And Paul uses the word of a church eating itself: “if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another” (Galatians 5:15) — congregations do not usually die of persecution.
webster_summary: To consume utterly. The devil goes about seeking whom he may devour, predators devour the poor, fire shall devour the adversaries — and a church that bites and devours itself will be consumed by itself.
webster_full: DEVOUR, v.t. [L. devoro; de and voro, to eat greedily.] To eat up; to eat with greediness; to eat ravenously, as a beast of prey.
2. To destroy; to consume with rapidity and violence; as, fire devours the buildings.
3. To destroy; to annihilate; to consume; as, to devour an estate.
4. To enjoy with avidity; as, to devour a book.
5. In Scripture, to slay; to waste; to ruin; to swallow up, Ps. 52.
corruption_summary: The devil is either dismissed as myth or made an all-seeing rival to God — while Galatians 5:15 goes unheeded, and churches that would resist any outside enemy consume themselves.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors surround 1 Peter 5:8. Liberal theology has treated the devil as a piece of primitive imagery to be demythologised, which leaves the New Testament's plainest warnings without a referent and makes our Lord's temptation a conversation with himself. The opposite error, common in charismatic circles, inflates him into a near-equal of God — everywhere at once, behind every difficulty, requiring elaborate techniques of warfare. Peter's language corrects both. The devil is real, personal, and dangerous; he is also a creature who must walk about and seek, and the prescribed response is not a technique but resistance stedfast in the faith, in the knowledge that the same afflictions are accomplished in the brethren everywhere.

The principle to recover is Galatians 5:15, which sits between a summary of the law in love and the works of the flesh. Paul knew that the church at greatest risk from biting and devouring was a church arguing about doctrine — the letter is a fierce defence of justification by faith, and even there he warns them about how they are treating each other. The warning has a grim logic: a congregation that consumes its own will not need an external enemy, because it will be consumed one of another. Contending earnestly for the faith and devouring one another are not the same activity, though they can look alike from inside.
roots_summary: Hebrew akal is to eat, and so to devour or consume; used of fire, of the sword, and of oppressors. Greek katapino is to drink down or swallow up; katesthio, to eat up.

Greek antidikos (G476) — an adversary at law, an opponent; Peter's title for the devil.

pos: v. (to pour out, especially blood; to spill or diffuse; rendering Hebrew shaphak, Greek ekcheo)
etymology: From the Saxon sceadan, to separate or divide, later to pour out. Hebrew shaphak is to pour out — used of blood, of wrath, and of the soul poured out in prayer — and the same verb serves for the pouring out of the Spirit.
biblical_def: Shed is the Bible's word for blood poured out, and everything turns on whose blood and why. The foundational statute is given to Noah for all mankind: “Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man” (Genesis 9:6). The reason clause is the whole argument — murder is capital because the victim bore God's image, so the sanctity of life and the penalty for taking it rest on the same fact. Proverbs lists among the seven things the LORD hates “a proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood” (Proverbs 6:17). Against that background our Lord takes a cup and says: “For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins” (Matthew 26:28). Innocent blood is shed — the very thing God hates — and it is shed by his own determinate counsel, for the remission of sins, and its beneficiaries are many. Then Paul uses the same verb for the gift that follows: “the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us” (Romans 5:5). Blood poured out at Calvary and love poured out in the heart are described by one word, and the second depends entirely on the first.
webster_summary: To pour out. Genesis makes shed blood capital because man bears God's image; God hates hands that shed innocent blood — and Christ's blood is shed for many, after which God's love is shed abroad in the heart.
webster_full: SHED, v.t. [Sax. sceadan, to separate, to pour out.] To cause to flow out; to pour out; to spill; to suffer to flow out; as, to shed tears.
2. To let fall; to cast; as, to shed the leaves or the hair.
3. To scatter; to emit; to throw off; to diffuse; as, flowers shed their fragrance.
4. SHED, v.i. To let fall its parts; as, the trees shed in autumn.
5. In Scripture, to shed blood, to slay; whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed, Gen. 9.
corruption_summary: The image-of-God ground of Genesis 9:6 is set aside, so that the taking of innocent life is argued on grounds of viability, capacity, or convenience rather than on what a man is.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 9:6 grounds the whole biblical doctrine of human life in a single clause: for in the image of God made he man. The value is not conferred by usefulness, capacity, consciousness, age, or the wishes of others, and it cannot be withdrawn by them. Every modern argument for taking innocent life — before birth, at its end, or for the sake of others' convenience — must first relocate human worth somewhere other than the image, usually in some measurable capacity. Once worth is made a matter of degree, some will always have less of it. Scripture's categories are simpler and harder: the unborn child is fearfully and wonderfully made and known before he was formed, and hands that shed innocent blood are among the things the LORD hates.

The principle to recover is what happened when innocent blood was shed at Calvary. Peter states both halves without flinching: Christ was delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, and by wicked hands crucified and slain (Acts 2:23). The greatest crime in history was also the appointed means of salvation, and neither fact cancels the other. What follows is the pouring of Romans 5:5, where the love of God is shed abroad in believers' hearts by the Holy Ghost. The order is fixed: blood shed first, love shed abroad after, and the second is the fruit of the first and never its cause.
roots_summary: Hebrew shaphak is to pour out — of blood, of wrath, and of the soul in prayer. Greek ekcheo is to pour out, used of Christ's blood and of the Spirit at Pentecost.
roots_lines: Hebrew shaphak (H8210) — to pour out; of blood shed, of wrath poured, and of the soul in prayer.
Hebrew dam (H1818) — blood; the life is in the blood, Leviticus 17:11.
Hebrew naqi (H5355) — innocent, clean; innocent blood in Proverbs 6:17.
Greek ekcheo (G1632) — to pour out; Christ's blood shed, and the Spirit poured out at Pentecost.
Greek aphesis (G859) — remission, release; the purpose named in Matthew 26:28.
